prize_parts.citation: for the development of palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling
for the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of DNA bases without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: Pd-catalysed C-N coupling is the clearest case on the shortlist of a general method that changed how chemists build bonds. Ligand design by Buchwald and by Hartwig turned a harsh, narrow aryl-amine synthesis into a routine operation that is now used daily in medicinal and process chemistry and appears in a very large number of later syntheses. Three decades of independent use, mechanistic work and industrial scale-up make it mature, and the 2010 cross-coupling prize did not cover C-N bond formation, so the achievement is distinct. I have moved my own view toward a two-part prize because the opening ballots show that base editing has the widest first-place support, and Liu's chemical contribution (evolved deaminases fused to a programmable nickase, with a clear mechanism and many independent replications) is real. Pairing a core molecule-making method with a chemical-biology invention would also stay within three laureates.
statement.case_against: B065 received only my own ballot as a first choice and the other seven members ranked it low or not at all, so its support is thin and may reflect nothing more than my own taste for synthesis. A committee could reasonably say that C-N coupling is an incremental extension of the 2010 palladium prize and that the history before it (Kosugi, Migita) makes the credit argument less clean than I stated. For base editing, the 2020 CRISPR prize sits close by, and a Liu-only part leaves out Komor, Gaudelli, Kondo and Nishida, which will be criticised. A prize combining two unrelated fields also lacks a unifying theme.

responses.point: Heiner ranks base editing first as a distinct chemical invention, not a refinement of cutting, with large generative impact, and suggests either Liu alone or Liu with Komor and Gaudelli.
responses.response: I agree that the deaminase-nickase fusion is a new chemical principle and not a cutting variant, which answers my worry about overlap with 2020. On attribution I side with a Liu-only part: Komor and Gaudelli did the founding experiments as lead trainees, but Nishida and Kondo reported a parallel cytidine editor, and including two trainees while excluding them invites a priority fight. A single laureate also leaves a place for Buchwald and Hartwig within the three-person limit, which a three-name base editing prize would not.

responses.point: Daniel ranks targeted protein degradation first as a genuinely new pharmacological modality, with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, and tests nominations by whether they changed what chemists and clinicians can do.
responses.response: I accept the modality argument, and that is why I list B011 as an alternative. My reservations are about timing and credit. No degrader is yet an approved drug, so the clinical consequence remains a promise. The PROTAC and the cereblon glue strands (Handa, Ito) are also parallel and partly separate, so three names would not honour the field. Seeing a stable credit split for B011 would be the main thing that moves it above B007 for me, and I would like to hear from you how you would deal with Handa and Ito.

responses.point: Emma ranks phase separation first as a new physical-chemical concept, with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen, while acknowledging that in vivo significance is still debated.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual reach, but this is the case where I ask what was new chemically, and I find the answer thin. The 2009 P-granule observation and multivalent demixing are strong results in cell biophysics, while the committee itself concedes that the definition of a condensate and its physiological relevance are contested. A prize should rest on settled interpretation, and I am not persuaded that B046 is there yet. I would be moved by evidence that the quantitative framework from Rosen, Pappu and Mittag now predicts behaviour in cells.

responses.point: Peter Brzezinski ranks nitrogenase first as a textbook problem in electron and proton transfer chemistry, with the crystal structures and the carbide assignment as lasting results.
responses.response: The FeMo-cofactor structure and the central carbide are impressive and independently confirmed, and I rank B028 as an alternative for that reason. My difficulty is that the catalytic cycle is still unresolved, so the work honoured would be largely structural, and Chabes and Zou make the same point. The credit is also spread over Rees, Einsle, Dean, Seefeldt and Ribbe over decades. I would support it more readily if you can show that the mechanism is now settled enough to carry a citation beyond structure.

responses.point: Xiaodong ranks halide perovskite solar absorbers first as designed inorganic architecture giving a new function, but accepts that stability and lead content are open and the three-person cut is contested.
responses.response: I agree that the structure-property story is neat and the device results are well reproduced. My reservation is about the credit cut: Miyasaka, Snaith and Park leave out Grätzel, Seok and Kanatzidis, who each made decisive steps, and I do not think any three-name choice would survive scrutiny. Unresolved stability also makes this an application whose practical consequence is not demonstrated. I would keep it behind both base editing and C-N coupling for now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards C-N coupling as too close to the 2010 cross-coupling prize, and whether Kosugi or Migita deserve any credit; my recollection of the early tin-amide history is not independently verified.
Whether a Liu-only base editing prize is acceptable given Komor, Gaudelli, Kondo and Nishida, or whether the committee would insist on more names.
Whether the PROTAC and molecular glue lines can be combined in a single three-person citation, and whether the lack of an approved degrader makes B011 premature.
Whether pairing two unrelated achievements is better than a single-theme prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of the shortlisted candidates is a former mentor, collaborator or colleague of mine. Masamune, my postdoctoral mentor, is not on the shortlist, and Lund colleagues Linke and Sparr are institutional peers, not candidates.
